subject: Biology
title: The Living World
summary: The opening chapter of Class 11 Biology: why the enormous diversity of living organisms has to be named and classified, the rules of binomial nomenclature, what taxonomy and systematics mean, and the seven taxonomic categories from species to kingdom with NCERT's standard examples (man, housefly, mango, wheat, the genus Panthera and the family Solanaceae). It is short and definition-heavy, and it is the vocabulary that every later chapter of Class 11, Class 12 and NEET assumes.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper. The Living World is the first chapter of Unit I, Diversity of Living Organisms (Chapters 1 to 4), which carries 15 marks in the CBSE Class 11 scheme. Because the chapter is small, it typically contributes 3 to 5 marks in the school final: an MCQ or an Assertion–Reason item, a 2-mark definition, and often one 3-mark question on nomenclature rules or the taxonomic hierarchy. In NEET, one or two questions from this chapter and Biological Classification together appear almost every year.

question_types.note: Identify the correctly written scientific name; the specific epithet in a given name; the correct ascending or descending order of categories; which plant category is equivalent to phylum (division); the suffix for family in plants (-aceae) and order (-ales); the genus of potato and brinjal (Solanum); who gave binomial nomenclature; what happens to common characters as you move from species to kingdom.

Species share more characters than a genus; Linn. after Mangifera indica means Linnaeus first described it; family Felidae and Canidae are together in order Carnivora; classification systems change because of new information; higher categories are harder to relate to other taxa at the same level.

Define taxon and category and distinguish them; taxonomy versus systematics; ICBN and ICZN in full; two rules of binomial nomenclature; scientific names of man, mango, wheat and housefly; why the name of the author is written after the specific epithet; state the two kingdoms named in the chapter.

All the rules of binomial nomenclature with an example; why living organisms are classified; why classification systems keep changing; the taxonomic hierarchy of one organism in full (man or mango are the favourites); explain species, genus and family with NCERT examples; what identification, nomenclature and classification mean.

Illustrate the taxonomic hierarchy with one plant and one animal (Table 1.1 of NCERT); explain all seven taxonomic categories in ascending order with examples and state the trend in the number of shared characters; a full account of nomenclature: need, codes, rules, example.

A passage or table listing the categories of man, housefly, mango and wheat, followed by sub-questions on which category a given name belongs to, which two organisms share a category, and why; or a passage on Panthera and Felis leading to questions on genus, family and order.

hot_topics: Rules of binomial nomenclature with Mangifera indica Linn. as the example
Taxonomic hierarchy of man, housefly, mango and wheat (NCERT Table 1.1)

Taxon versus category; taxonomy versus systematics
Why organisms are classified and why classification systems change

Trend in shared characters and number of organisms as you go up the hierarchy

sections.heading: 1.1 Diversity in the Living World: biodiversity and the need to name and classify
sections.body:
NCERT starts with a simple observation. Look around you and you find an enormous variety of living organisms, and the variety multiplies the moment you widen your search to a forest, a lake or the sea. Every new area shows organisms you have not seen before. The number of species that are known and described lies between 1.7 and 1.8 million. This number and variety of organisms present on earth is what the chapter calls biodiversity. A large number of organisms still remain unknown, so the number keeps rising as new ones are described.

Two problems follow at once from such variety. First, how do you refer to an organism so that a scientist anywhere in the world knows exactly which one you mean? Local names change from place to place, and one plant can carry different names in different regions, or one name can be used for different plants. So there has to be a standardised way of naming, which NCERT calls nomenclature. Second, with millions of kinds, you cannot study each one on its own; you need to put them into groups. That is classification.

One more step comes before naming, and students often skip it: identification. Nomenclature is possible only when the organism has been correctly described and you know to which organism the name is attached. The order the examiner wants is identification, then nomenclature, then classification. NCERT summarises it as the processes basic to taxonomy: characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature.

Why classify at all? Because classification lets you study a small sample and apply what you learn to the whole group, it makes the study of the enormous diversity manageable, and it shows the relationships between different groups. NCERT exercise Q1 (why are living organisms classified) and Q2 (why do classification systems keep changing) are straight from this paragraph and are asked almost every year.
sections.tip: If asked why the classification systems keep changing, the key point is that classification is based on the characters chosen; earlier systems used a few easily observed external characters, and as knowledge of internal structure, cells, development, genetics and evolutionary relationships grew, the criteria changed and so did the systems.

sections.heading: 1.1 Diversity in the Living World: nomenclature and the rules of binomial nomenclature
sections.body:
Biologists have agreed on principles so that each organism gets a scientific name that is accepted everywhere and used by everyone. For plants the rules are laid down in the International Code for Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN), and for animals in the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN). The aim is stated exactly in NCERT: a scientific name ensures that each organism has only one name, and that no other organism has the same name.

The system in use is binomial nomenclature, given by Carolus Linnaeus. Every name has two components: the generic name and the specific epithet. In Mangifera indica, the mango, Mangifera is the genus and indica is the specific epithet. Write the rules as a numbered list; the marking scheme rewards each one.

  1. Biological names are generally in Latin and written in italics. They are Latinised or derived from Latin irrespective of their origin.
  2. The first word represents the genus; the second is the specific epithet.
  3. When handwritten, both words are separately underlined; when printed they are in italics, to indicate their Latin origin.
  4. The genus starts with a capital letter; the specific epithet starts with a small letter.

A fifth point that examiners like: the name of the author appears after the specific epithet, at the end of the name, in an abbreviated form. Mangifera indica Linn. tells you that the species was first described by Linnaeus. The author's name is not italicised or underlined.

Common examples you should be able to write correctly: man Homo sapiens; mango Mangifera indica; potato Solanum tuberosum; brinjal Solanum melongena; lion Panthera leo; tiger Panthera tigris; leopard Panthera pardus; housefly Musca domestica; wheat Triticum aestivum. A specific epithet can appear under more than one genus (indica is common), but the two-word combination is unique.
sections.tip: In the exam you are handwriting, so underline the two words separately: Mangifera and indica each get their own line. A single underline under the whole name, or a capital I in Indica, loses the mark. NCERT exercise Q5 tests exactly this.

sections.heading: 1.1 Diversity in the Living World: classification, taxonomy and systematics
sections.body:
Classification, in NCERT's words, is the process by which anything is grouped into convenient categories based on some easily observable characters. When we say plants or animals, dogs or cats, insects, we are already using categories. The scientific term for these categories is taxa (singular taxon). Notice that taxa can be at very different levels: plants, wheat, animals, mammals and dogs are all taxa, but wheat is a much smaller group than plants, and dogs a much smaller group than mammals. So classification is not just naming a group; it involves ranking groups relative to each other.

Taxonomy is the branch that does this work. Its processes are characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature. Modern taxonomy does not depend on external appearance alone; NCERT says organisms are classified on the basis of external and internal structure, along with the structure of the cell, the development process and ecological information.

People classified organisms long before there was a science of taxonomy, because they needed to know which plants and animals were useful for food, shelter and clothing. The systematic study that grew out of that interest is systematics. The word comes from the Latin systema, meaning a systematic arrangement of organisms; Linnaeus used Systema Naturae as the title of his publication. Systematics includes identification, nomenclature and classification, and, in addition, it takes into account the evolutionary relationships between organisms. That last phrase is the difference the examiner wants when asked to distinguish taxonomy from systematics.

A frequently tested pair is taxon versus category. A category is the rank (species, genus, family and so on); a taxon is the actual group of organisms placed at that rank. Mammalia is a taxon at the rank of class; Solanaceae is a taxon at the rank of family. Keep this distinction ready for a 2-mark question.
sections.tip: Two-mark question: 'Distinguish between taxonomy and systematics.' Write that systematics includes all that taxonomy does (identification, nomenclature, classification) plus the study of evolutionary relationships among organisms, and name the origin of the word (Latin systema, Linnaeus's Systema Naturae).

sections.heading: 1.2 Taxonomic Categories: the hierarchy
sections.body:
Classification is not a single-step process. It involves a hierarchy of steps, and each step represents a rank or category. Since a category is part of the overall taxonomic arrangement, it is called a taxonomic category, and all the categories together constitute the taxonomic hierarchy. Each category is a unit of classification, and each represents a rank; NCERT says it is commonly termed a taxon.

NCERT illustrates with insects. Insects share a common feature, three pairs of jointed legs, so the group 'insects' represents a class. NCERT stresses that taxonomic categories are distinct biological entities, not merely morphological aggregates: a category is a real group of organisms that share features because they are related, not just a pile of things that happen to look alike.

The categories every student must know, in ascending order, are: species → genus → family → order → class → phylum (division for plants) → kingdom. Species is at the lowest end of the hierarchy and kingdom at the top. To place an organism in the categories, you must know the characters of the individual or group and identify the similarities and dissimilarities with other organisms.

Two trends run through the whole hierarchy and are asked in almost every paper. First, as you go higher from species to kingdom, the number of common characteristics goes on decreasing: the lower the taxon, the more characters its members share. Second, the number of organisms included in a taxon increases as you go up; a species contains fewer organisms than its genus, a genus fewer than its family, and so on. NCERT adds a consequence: the higher the category, the greater the difficulty in determining the relationship of that taxon to other taxa at the same level, so the problem of classification becomes more complex at higher ranks.

Every organism is placed in all seven categories at once. This is the reason a scientific name, which uses only the genus and species, is enough to locate the organism in the entire hierarchy.
sections.tip: When a question asks for the sequence, write the arrow chain both ways only if asked; otherwise write it ascending from species and label division in brackets next to phylum. Missing 'division for plants' is a common half-mark loss.

sections.heading: 1.2.1 Species
sections.body:
NCERT defines a species as a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities. It is the lowest category of the taxonomic hierarchy and the basic unit of classification. Closely related species can be distinguished from one another on the basis of distinct morphological differences.

The standard examples are Mangifera indica (mango), Solanum tuberosum (potato) and Panthera leo (lion). In each name the second word, indica, tuberosum and leo, is the specific epithet, while Mangifera, Solanum and Panthera are the genera. A genus may contain one or more specific epithets, each representing a different organism, but the organisms share morphological similarities. So Panthera has another species, Panthera tigris (tiger), and Solanum includes Solanum nigrum and Solanum melongena (brinjal) in addition to potato. Human beings belong to the species sapiens in the genus Homo, so the scientific name is Homo sapiens.

Exercise Q8 asks you to collect the currently accepted meanings of the word species. The taxonomic meaning, which is what NCERT uses here, is a group of organisms that share fundamental similarities and can be distinguished from related groups by morphology. The biological meaning, which you will meet in Class 12 Evolution, is a group of natural populations whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring and which are reproductively isolated from other such groups. Outside biology the word is used more loosely: in chemistry a species is any kind of atom, ion or molecule under discussion, and in everyday speech it means simply a kind or sort. The point of the exercise is that in biology the word has a precise meaning, the lowest taxonomic category.

Exemplar asks what makes potato and brinjal separate species though both are Solanum. The answer: they share the generic characters that place them in Solanum, but they differ in distinct, stable morphological features (the tuber-bearing underground stem of potato, the fruit and floral details of brinjal), and they do not interbreed, so they are separate species within the same genus.
sections.tip: Never write the specific epithet alone as a name. 'indica' or 'sapiens' by itself identifies nothing; the name is always genus plus specific epithet.

sections.heading: 1.2.2 Genus
sections.body:
A genus comprises a group of related species which have more characters in common when compared with species of other genera. NCERT's phrase is that genera are aggregates of closely related species. The genus is the category just above species and gives the first word of the binomial name.

Plant example: potato and brinjal are two different species, but both belong to the genus Solanum, because they share the floral and vegetative features that define that genus. Animal example: lion (Panthera leo), leopard (Panthera pardus) and tiger (Panthera tigris) have several common features and are all species of the genus Panthera. This genus differs from another genus, Felis, which includes the cats. The contrast between Panthera and Felis is the example the examiner expects when you are asked to explain genus; it also sets up the next category, because both genera will be placed together in one family.

Points to remember for marks: a genus can contain a single species or many; all species of a genus share the generic name; species of the same genus resemble each other more than they resemble species of other genera; and the genus name, when written alone, is still a valid taxon (you can say the genus Panthera), whereas the specific epithet alone is not.

A short comparison that answers many 2-mark questions: species is a group of individuals with fundamental similarities and is the lowest category; genus is a group of related species with more characters in common than with species of other genera and is the next higher category. The number of shared characters is greater within a species than within a genus.
sections.tip: When you write P. tigris after having written Panthera leo in full once, the abbreviation is acceptable, but in an exam it is safer to write the genus in full each time.

sections.heading: 1.2.3 Family
sections.body:
A family is a group of related genera with still fewer similarities as compared to genus and species. In plants, families are characterised on the basis of both vegetative and reproductive features of the plant species. The reproductive features (flower, fruit, seed) are more stable and are the main basis of plant families, which is why the same family can include plants that look very different vegetatively.

Plant example: three different genera, Solanum, Petunia and Datura, are placed in the family Solanaceae. Animal example: the genus Panthera, comprising lion, tiger and leopard, is put along with the genus Felis (cats) in the family Felidae. NCERT then makes the comparison the other way: if you look at the features of a cat and a dog, you find some similarities and some differences, and they are separated into two different families, Felidae and Canidae.

The naming pattern is worth memorising because it appears as an MCQ. Plant family names end in -aceae (Solanaceae, Poaceae, Anacardiaceae, Convolvulaceae). Animal family names end in -idae (Felidae, Canidae, Hominidae, Muscidae). The suffix tells you the rank at a glance.

Families of the four NCERT organisms: man belongs to Hominidae, housefly to Muscidae, mango to Anacardiaceae and wheat to Poaceae. Learn these four as a set with their orders, because the 5-mark hierarchy question can be asked about any of them.
sections.tip: If asked to give two genera of the family Solanaceae, write Solanum and Petunia (or Datura). If asked for two families of the order Carnivora, write Felidae and Canidae. Keep the pairs straight; mixing plant and animal examples in one answer is a common error.

sections.heading: 1.2.4 Order
sections.body:
Order and the categories above it are identified on the basis of an aggregate of characters. An order is an assemblage of families which exhibit a few similar characters. The similar characters are fewer in number than those of the different genera included in a family; that is the sentence NCERT uses and it is the sentence the marking scheme carries.

Plant example: the families Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae are included in the order Polymoniales, mainly on the basis of floral characters. Animal example: the order Carnivora includes the families Felidae and Canidae. So cats, lions, tigers, leopards and dogs are all Carnivora, even though they sit in two families and several genera.

Plant order names end in -ales (Polymoniales, Sapindales, Poales). Animal order names have no fixed suffix (Carnivora, Primata, Diptera), so learn them as words. The orders of the four NCERT organisms: man in Primata, housefly in Diptera, mango in Sapindales, wheat in Poales.

A typical 3-mark question asks you to explain why an order shows fewer common characters than a family. The answer runs through the logic of the hierarchy: a family is a group of related genera, so its members already share fewer characters than the species within one genus; an order groups several such families, and the only characters common to all of them are the few that all the families happen to share. Each step up unites more diverse groups on fewer shared characters. Use the Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae example to make it concrete: within Solanaceae the genera share many floral and vegetative characters; across the order Polymoniales only a few floral characters are common.
sections.tip: Spell the order as NCERT does: Polymoniales. Examiners marking from the NCERT key expect the NCERT spelling.

sections.heading: 1.2.5 Class
sections.body:
A class includes related orders. NCERT's example is from the animal side. The order Primata, comprising monkey, gorilla and gibbon, is placed in the class Mammalia along with the order Carnivora, which includes animals like tiger, cat and dog. The class Mammalia has other orders as well; the two named are only examples. What unites all the orders in Mammalia is the set of mammalian characters (mammary glands, hair, and the other features you will meet in Animal Kingdom), which are shared by monkeys and dogs alike even though those animals belong to different orders and families.

The earlier insect example is also a class: insects, with three pairs of jointed legs, form the class Insecta, to which the housefly belongs. For plants, the classes named in Table 1.1 are Dicotyledonae (mango) and Monocotyledonae (wheat), based on the number of cotyledons in the seed along with other characters.

Classes of the four NCERT organisms: man in Mammalia, housefly in Insecta, mango in Dicotyledonae, wheat in Monocotyledonae.

At this level of the hierarchy the number of organisms in a taxon is very large and the shared characters are few but fundamental. This is a good place to remember the second trend: a class like Mammalia contains many orders, each order many families, each family many genera, each genus one or more species, so the count of organisms rises steeply as you climb. If a question asks which taxon has the largest number of organisms, the highest category listed in the options is the answer; if it asks which has the most characters in common, the lowest category is the answer.
sections.tip: Do not confuse the order Primata with the class Mammalia in the hierarchy of man; the sequence is Homo sapiens, Homo, Hominidae, Primata, Mammalia, Chordata, Animalia.

sections.heading: 1.2.6 Phylum (Division in plants)
sections.body:
Classes comprising animals like fishes, amphibians, reptiles and birds, along with mammals, constitute the next higher category, the phylum. All of these are included in the phylum Chordata on the basis of common features such as the presence of a notochord and a dorsal hollow neural system. NCERT names these two characters and an MCQ on the shared features of Chordata is common; give both.

In plants, classes with a few similar characters are assigned to the higher category called a division. Division is the plant equivalent of phylum, and this equivalence is one of the most repeated 1-mark questions from the chapter (NCERT Exemplar asks it directly). In Table 1.1 both mango and wheat are placed in the division Angiospermae, the flowering plants, even though one is a dicot and the other a monocot.

Phylum or division of the four NCERT organisms: man in Chordata, housefly in Arthropoda, mango in Angiospermae, wheat in Angiospermae. Arthropoda, which the housefly shares with crabs, spiders and all other jointed-legged animals, is the largest phylum of the animal kingdom, a fact used in Animal Kingdom later.

The phylum is the level at which the characters shared are the broad body-plan features rather than details. A fish and a human share a notochord at some stage of development and a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and little else that is obvious; that is enough to put them in one phylum. This is exactly what NCERT means when it says the higher the category, the fewer the shared characters and the harder it is to determine relationships among taxa at that level.
sections.tip: Write 'Phylum / Division' as the label in any hierarchy diagram, and when the organism is a plant, write Division only. Writing 'phylum Angiospermae' is marked wrong by a strict examiner.

sections.heading: 1.2.7 Kingdom
sections.body:
All animals belonging to the various phyla are assigned to the highest category, the kingdom Animalia, and all plants to the kingdom Plantae. These are the two kingdoms named in this chapter; the five-kingdom classification of Whittaker with Monera, Protista and Fungi comes in Chapter 2, Biological Classification. Kingdom is the top of the hierarchy and contains the greatest number of organisms with the fewest shared characters.

NCERT closes the chapter with Table 1.1, which every student should be able to reproduce from memory. Read it as four columns.

  • Man: species Homo sapiens, genus Homo, family Hominidae, order Primata, class Mammalia, phylum Chordata, kingdom Animalia.
  • Housefly: species Musca domestica, genus Musca, family Muscidae, order Diptera, class Insecta, phylum Arthropoda, kingdom Animalia.
  • Mango: species Mangifera indica, genus Mangifera, family Anacardiaceae, order Sapindales, class Dicotyledonae, division Angiospermae, kingdom Plantae.
  • Wheat: species Triticum aestivum, genus Triticum, family Poaceae, order Poales, class Monocotyledonae, division Angiospermae, kingdom Plantae.

Notice what the table teaches. Man and housefly share only the kingdom. Mango and wheat share the division and the kingdom but part at the class. Exercise Q11 (illustrate the taxonomic hierarchy with a plant and an animal) is answered by writing any one plant column and any one animal column of this table, preferably as a flow chart from species to kingdom.

NCERT ends with the observation that the problem of classification becomes more complex as you go higher, because each higher category contains more organisms sharing fewer characters, and so determining how one taxon relates to the others at the same rank becomes progressively harder. That sentence is the conclusion of the chapter and makes a good last line for any long answer on the hierarchy.
sections.tip: For a 5-mark hierarchy question, draw a vertical flow chart with seven boxes, put the category name on the left and the taxon for your organism on the right, and add the arrow with 'number of common characters decreases' pointing upward. That single annotation often earns the last mark.

key_terms.definition: The number and types of organisms present on earth. The known and described species number between 1.7 and 1.8 million.
Determining the correct name and place of an organism by comparing its characters with those already described. It must precede nomenclature and classification.
The standardised system of naming organisms so that each has only one name and no other organism carries the same name; governed by ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals.
The two-word naming system given by Carolus Linnaeus, in which the first word is the generic name and the second is the specific epithet, e.g. Mangifera indica.
The second word of a scientific name, written in small letters, which along with the genus identifies the species, e.g. indica in Mangifera indica.
The process by which anything is grouped into convenient categories based on some easily observable characters.

The branch of biology dealing with characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature of organisms, based on external and internal structure, cell structure, development and ecological information.
The systematic study of organisms (from Latin systema) that includes identification, nomenclature and classification and also takes into account evolutionary relationships between organisms.
A unit of classification; any group of organisms placed at a particular rank, e.g. Mammalia, Solanaceae, Panthera. Plural taxa.
A rank or level in the hierarchy of classification, such as species, genus, family, order, class, phylum or division and kingdom.
The arrangement of all taxonomic categories in a sequence of ranks from species at the bottom to kingdom at the top.
A group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities; the lowest taxonomic category and the basic unit of classification.
A group of related species that have more characters in common when compared with species of other genera; an aggregate of closely related species, e.g. Panthera, Solanum.
A group of related genera with fewer similarities than a genus, characterised in plants by both vegetative and reproductive features, e.g. Solanaceae, Felidae.
An assemblage of families exhibiting a few similar characters, e.g. Polymoniales (Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae), Carnivora (Felidae and Canidae).
A group of related orders, e.g. Mammalia containing Primata and Carnivora.
A group of related classes; called phylum in animals (Chordata, Arthropoda) and division in plants (Angiospermae).
The highest taxonomic category, containing all phyla (Animalia) or all divisions (Plantae) of the group.

formula_sheet.name: Number of known species
formula_sheet.note: This variety is called biodiversity; many organisms remain undescribed.

formula_sheet.name: Ascending order of categories
formula_sheet.expr: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum (Division in plants) → Kingdom
formula_sheet.note: Species at the lowest end, kingdom at the top.

formula_sheet.name: Trend up the hierarchy
formula_sheet.expr: Shared characters decrease; number of organisms in the taxon increases; relationships harder to determine
formula_sheet.note: Lower the taxon, more the characters its members share.

formula_sheet.name: Rules of binomial nomenclature
formula_sheet.expr: Latin, italics; first word genus, second specific epithet; handwritten names underlined separately; genus capital, epithet small letter; author's abbreviated name after the epithet (Mangifera indica Linn.)

formula_sheet.name: Nomenclature codes
formula_sheet.expr: ICBN = International Code for Botanical Nomenclature (plants); ICZN = International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (animals)
formula_sheet.note: Ensure one name per organism and no name shared by two organisms.

formula_sheet.name: Systematics
formula_sheet.expr: Latin systema = systematic arrangement; Linnaeus's Systema Naturae; taxonomy + evolutionary relationships
formula_sheet.note: The extra element over taxonomy is evolutionary relationships.

formula_sheet.name: Hierarchy of man
formula_sheet.expr: Homo sapiens · Homo · Hominidae · Primata · Mammalia · Chordata · Animalia

formula_sheet.name: Hierarchy of housefly
formula_sheet.expr: Musca domestica · Musca · Muscidae · Diptera · Insecta · Arthropoda · Animalia

formula_sheet.name: Hierarchy of mango
formula_sheet.expr: Mangifera indica · Mangifera · Anacardiaceae · Sapindales · Dicotyledonae · Angiospermae · Plantae
formula_sheet.note: Angiospermae is a division, not a phylum.

formula_sheet.name: Hierarchy of wheat
formula_sheet.expr: Triticum aestivum · Triticum · Poaceae · Poales · Monocotyledonae · Angiospermae · Plantae
formula_sheet.note: Mango and wheat share division and kingdom only.

formula_sheet.name: Genus and family examples
formula_sheet.expr: Panthera (leo, tigris, pardus) + Felis → Felidae; Felidae + Canidae → Carnivora; Solanum (tuberosum, melongena, nigrum) + Petunia + Datura → Solanaceae; Solanaceae + Convolvulaceae → Polymoniales
formula_sheet.note: The examiner's favourite examples for genus, family and order.

formula_sheet.name: Class Mammalia example
formula_sheet.expr: Order Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) + order Carnivora (tiger, cat, dog) → class Mammalia

formula_sheet.name: Phylum Chordata characters
formula_sheet.expr: Presence of notochord and dorsal hollow neural system
formula_sheet.note: Unites fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

formula_sheet.name: Suffixes
formula_sheet.expr: Plant family -aceae; plant order -ales; animal family -idae
formula_sheet.note: A quick way to identify the rank of a name in an MCQ.

diagrams.title: Taxonomic categories showing hierarchical arrangement in ascending order (NCERT Figure 1.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw seven boxes stacked vertically with an upward arrow running beside them. From bottom to top label the boxes Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum (Division), Kingdom. Along the arrow write 'ascending order'. On the right add two annotations: 'number of common characters decreases' with an upward arrow, and 'number of organisms increases' with an upward arrow. Give the title exactly as in NCERT.

diagrams.title: Taxonomic hierarchy of man (Homo sapiens)
diagrams.how_to_draw: A flow chart of seven boxes from top to bottom or bottom to top, each with the category on the left and the taxon on the right: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Primata, Family Hominidae, Genus Homo, Species sapiens (write the full name Homo sapiens underlined separately). Connect the boxes with arrows. Underline the genus and species names.

diagrams.title: Taxonomic hierarchy of mango (Mangifera indica)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Same seven-box flow chart: Kingdom Plantae, Division Angiospermae, Class Dicotyledonae, Order Sapindales, Family Anacardiaceae, Genus Mangifera, Species indica (full name Mangifera indica underlined separately). Write 'Division' and not 'Phylum' for the plant. This plus the man chart answers NCERT exercise Q11 completely.

diagrams.title: Taxonomic hierarchy of housefly (Musca domestica)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Seven boxes: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Arthropoda, Class Insecta, Order Diptera, Family Muscidae, Genus Musca, Species domestica. Add a note beside class Insecta: three pairs of jointed legs, the character NCERT uses to define the class.

diagrams.title: Taxonomic hierarchy of wheat (Triticum aestivum)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Seven boxes: Kingdom Plantae, Division Angiospermae, Class Monocotyledonae, Order Poales, Family Poaceae, Genus Triticum, Species aestivum. ncert_questions.a:
Living organisms are classified because of the following reasons.

  • The number of living organisms is enormous (1.7 to 1.8 million species are already known and described) and they show great diversity in form, habitat and behaviour. It is impossible to study each of them individually.
  • Classification groups organisms into convenient categories on the basis of shared, easily observable characters, so that the characters of a whole group can be understood by studying a few of its members.
  • It makes identification and naming of organisms possible and gives every organism a definite place in the hierarchy.
  • It reveals relationships and evolutionary affinities among different groups of organisms.
  • It provides a common reference that scientists all over the world can use, and it helps in the study of organisms of economic, medical and agricultural importance.

ncert_questions.q: Why are the classification systems changing every now and then?
ncert_questions.a: Classification is based on the characters chosen for grouping organisms, and these have changed with time. The earliest systems used a few easily observed external characters such as habit, habitat and gross morphology. As knowledge grew, biologists started using internal structure (anatomy), the structure of the cell, the process of development, biochemistry, genetics and ecological information. Systematics also began to consider the evolutionary relationships between organisms. Each time a new kind of evidence became available, or a new organism was discovered that did not fit the existing groups, the criteria of classification were revised and the systems changed. So classification systems are dynamic; they keep changing because our understanding of the characteristics and relationships of organisms keeps improving.

ncert_questions.q: What different criteria would you choose to classify people whom you meet often?
ncert_questions.a: People can be grouped on the basis of simple observable criteria, for example: age (children, adults, elderly); sex; place of residence (locality, town, state); occupation (students, teachers, doctors, shopkeepers); relationship (family members, friends, neighbours, classmates); physical features such as height, complexion and colour of hair; language spoken; and interests such as sports or music. The purpose of the question is to show that any classification depends on the criteria you choose, and that the same set of people can be grouped in many different ways, just as organisms can.

ncert_questions.q: What do we learn from the identification of individuals and populations?
ncert_questions.a: Identification of an individual tells us its correct name and its place in the taxonomic hierarchy: its species, genus, family and so on, and therefore the characters it shares with the other members of those taxa. Identification of populations tells us about the range of variation within a species, the habitats in which it lives and its geographical distribution. Together these give us information on the relationships and evolutionary affinities between organisms, allow us to describe new species when an individual does not match any known one, and help in recognising organisms that are useful (food, medicine) or harmful (pests, disease vectors).

ncert_questions.q: Given below is the scientific name of Mango. Identify the correctly written name. (a) Mangifera Indica (b) Mangifera indica
ncert_questions.a: (b) Mangifera indica is correct. In binomial nomenclature the first word (genus) begins with a capital letter and the second word (specific epithet) begins with a small letter. Both words are printed in italics or, when handwritten, underlined separately. In (a) the specific epithet has been wrongly written with a capital I.

ncert_questions.q: Define a taxon. Give some examples of taxa at different hierarchical levels.
ncert_questions.a:
A taxon is a unit of classification; it is any group of organisms placed at a particular rank or category in the taxonomic hierarchy. Each category of the hierarchy represents a taxon.

Examples at different levels: kingdom Plantae and kingdom Animalia; phylum Chordata and division Angiospermae; class Mammalia and class Insecta; order Primata and order Carnivora; family Solanaceae and family Felidae; genus Panthera and genus Solanum; species Homo sapiens and Mangifera indica.

ncert_questions.q: Can you identify the correct sequence of taxonomical categories? (a) Species → Order → Phylum → Kingdom (b) Genus → Species → Order → Kingdom (c) Species → Genus → Order → Phylum
ncert_questions.a: (c) Species → Genus → Order → Phylum is the correct ascending sequence. The full order of categories from lowest to highest is species, genus, family, order, class, phylum (division), kingdom. Option (b) is wrong because genus lies above species, not below it. Option (a) also runs upward but jumps from species straight to order, leaving out genus; (c) is the accepted answer because it moves from species through the very next category, genus, and then upward.

ncert_questions.q: Try to collect all the currently accepted meanings for the word species. Discuss with your teacher the meaning of species in the case of higher plants and animals on one hand, and bacteria on the other hand.
ncert_questions.a:
Accepted meanings of the word species:

  • Taxonomic (morphological) species: a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities, which can be distinguished from closely related groups by distinct morphological differences. This is the definition used in this chapter and is the lowest taxonomic category.
  • Biological species: a group of natural populations whose members can interbreed among themselves and produce fertile offspring, and which are reproductively isolated from other such groups.
  • In chemistry and physics, species means any kind of atom, ion, molecule or particle under discussion; in ordinary language it means a kind or sort.

For higher plants and animals the biological concept works well, because sexual reproduction and reproductive isolation can be tested; the species is defined by interbreeding ability plus morphology. For bacteria the biological concept fails, because bacteria reproduce asexually and exchange genes across groups. Bacterial species are therefore defined on the basis of morphological, biochemical, physiological and molecular (DNA sequence) similarity rather than interbreeding.

ncert_questions.q: Define and understand the following terms: (i) Phylum (ii) Class (iii) Family (iv) Order (v) Genus
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Phylum: a group of related classes sharing a few fundamental characters. Classes of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals form the phylum Chordata on the basis of a notochord and a dorsal hollow neural system. In plants the equivalent category is division (Angiospermae).

(ii) Class: a group of related orders. Order Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) and order Carnivora (tiger, cat, dog) are placed in class Mammalia.

(iii) Family: a group of related genera with fewer similarities than a genus or species; in plants it is based on both vegetative and reproductive characters. Solanum, Petunia and Datura are in family Solanaceae; Panthera and Felis are in family Felidae.

(iv) Order: an assemblage of families which exhibit a few similar characters, fewer than those shared within a family. Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae are in order Polymoniales; Felidae and Canidae are in order Carnivora.

(v) Genus: a group of related species with more characters in common than with species of other genera; an aggregate of closely related species. Lion, tiger and leopard are species of Panthera; potato and brinjal are species of Solanum.

ncert_questions.q: How is a key helpful in the identification and classification of an organism?
ncert_questions.a: A key is a taxonomic aid used to identify plants and animals on the basis of similarities and dissimilarities. It is made of pairs of contrasting characters called couplets; each statement in a couplet is a lead. The user reads the two leads, chooses the one that matches the organism, and is directed to the next couplet, and so on, until the organism is identified. Because one of the two contrasting characters is accepted and the other rejected at each step, the key narrows down the possibilities quickly and objectively. Separate keys are prepared for each taxonomic category (family, genus, species), and keys are generally analytical in nature. In this way a key allows a student or a researcher to identify an unknown organism and place it in the correct taxon without needing an expert.

ncert_questions.q: Illustrate the taxonomical hierarchy with suitable examples of a plant and an animal.
ncert_questions.a:
The taxonomic hierarchy is the arrangement of categories in ascending order: species, genus, family, order, class, phylum (division in plants), kingdom. As we go up, the number of common characters decreases and the number of organisms in each taxon increases.

Plant, mango: kingdom Plantae → division Angiospermae → class Dicotyledonae → order Sapindales → family Anacardiaceae → genus Mangifera → species indica. Scientific name Mangifera indica.

Animal, man: kingdom Animalia → phylum Chordata → class Mammalia → order Primata → family Hominidae → genus Homo → species sapiens. Scientific name Homo sapiens.

(In the exam draw the two as vertical flow charts side by side with the category names written between them. Wheat, Triticum aestivum: Plantae, Angiospermae, Monocotyledonae, Poales, Poaceae, Triticum, aestivum; or housefly, Musca domestica: Animalia, Arthropoda, Insecta, Diptera, Muscidae, Musca, domestica, may be used instead.)

ncert_questions.q: Brassica campestris Linn. (a) Give the common name of the plant. (b) What do the first two parts of the name denote? (c) Why are they written in italics? (d) What is the meaning of Linn. written at the end of the name?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) The plant is mustard (sarson).

(b) Brassica is the generic name (genus) and campestris is the specific epithet; together they form the binomial name of the species.

(c) Both words are written in italics (or underlined separately when handwritten) to indicate their Latin origin, as required by the rules of binomial nomenclature.

(d) Linn. is the abbreviated name of the author, Linnaeus, written after the specific epithet to indicate that Linnaeus first described this species.

ncert_questions.q: Brinjal and potato belong to the same genus Solanum, but to two different species. What defines them as separate species?
ncert_questions.a: Members of the same genus share many characters, which is why brinjal (Solanum melongena) and potato (Solanum tuberosum) are placed together in Solanum. A species, however, is a group of individuals with fundamental similarities that can be distinguished from closely related species by distinct morphological differences. Brinjal and potato differ in stable, heritable morphological features: potato bears underground stem tubers and its fruit is small and inedible, while brinjal has no tubers and bears a large edible berry; the leaf, flower and seed characters also differ. Further, they do not interbreed in nature to produce fertile offspring. These distinct morphological differences and reproductive isolation define them as two separate species within one genus.

ncert_questions.q: A plant may have different names in different regions of the country or world. How do botanists solve this problem?
ncert_questions.a: Local or vernacular names vary from region to region and language to language, so the same plant may have many names and one name may refer to different plants. Botanists solve this by giving every plant a single scientific name under the rules of the International Code for Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN), using the binomial nomenclature of Linnaeus. The name has two Latin or Latinised words, the genus and the specific epithet, written in italics or underlined separately, with the genus capitalised and the epithet in small letters; for example the mango is Mangifera indica everywhere in the world. The code ensures that each plant has only one valid scientific name and that no two plants share a name, so scientists anywhere can communicate without confusion.

ncert_questions.q: What is the difference between a taxon and a category?
ncert_questions.a: A category is a rank or level in the taxonomic hierarchy, such as species, genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom; it is abstract and has no organisms of its own. A taxon is the actual group of organisms placed at a given rank; it is a concrete biological entity. For example, class is a category, whereas Mammalia is a taxon at the rank of class; family is a category, whereas Solanaceae is a taxon at the rank of family.

ncert_questions.q: Linnaeus is considered as the Father of Taxonomy. Name two other botanists known for their contribution to the field of plant taxonomy. Also state what ICZN stands for.
ncert_questions.a: Two other botanists known for their contribution to plant taxonomy are George Bentham and Joseph Dalton Hooker, who gave the natural system of classification of seed plants. ICZN stands for International Code of Zoological Nomenclature, the set of rules for naming animals; the corresponding code for plants is ICBN, the International Code for Botanical Nomenclature.

pyq.q: As we go from species to kingdom in a taxonomic hierarchy, the number of common characteristics
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The lower the taxon, the more characters its members share. Going up from species to kingdom, each category unites more diverse groups on fewer shared characters, so the number of common characters decreases.

pyq.q: The term systematics refers to
options: identification and classification of plants and animals only
the diversity of kinds of organisms and their relationships
the naming of organisms in Latin
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Systematics includes identification, nomenclature and classification and, in addition, the evolutionary relationships between organisms; it is the study of the kinds of organisms and their relationships.

pyq.q: A genus represents
options: a collection of unrelated plants or animals
a group of closely related species of plants or animals
the lowest category of the taxonomic hierarchy
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: NCERT defines a genus as an aggregate of closely related species having more characters in common than with species of other genera; species, not genus, is the lowest category.

pyq.q: The taxonomic unit phylum in the classification of animals is equivalent to which hierarchical level in the classification of plants?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: In plants, classes with a few similar characters are assigned to a higher category called division, which corresponds to phylum in animals.

pyq.q: Which of the following taxa contains the largest number of organisms?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The number of organisms in a taxon increases as we go up the hierarchy; kingdom is the highest category and includes all the phyla or divisions below it.

pyq.q: Identify the correct sequence of taxonomic categories in ascending order.
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The full ascending order is species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom; only option (c) keeps every listed category in the correct relative position.

pyq.q: Which of the following is the correctly written scientific name of the mango?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The genus begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter, and both are italicised or underlined separately.

pyq.q: Which of the following suffixes used for units of classification in plants indicates the taxonomic category of family?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Plant family names end in -aceae (Solanaceae, Poaceae); -ales marks a plant order (Poales, Sapindales).

pyq.q: Potato, brinjal and Solanum nigrum are placed in the same
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Solanum tuberosum (potato), Solanum melongena (brinjal) and Solanum nigrum are three species of the single genus Solanum, family Solanaceae.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Solanum tuberosum and Solanum melongena are placed in the same genus. Reason (R): Species of one genus have more characters in common than they share with species of other genera.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Potato and brinjal are two species of Solanum precisely because they share the generic characters more closely with each other than with species of other genera, which is the NCERT definition of a genus.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): In Mangifera indica Linn., Linn. is written after the specific epithet. Reason (R): The abbreviated name of the author who first described the species is written at the end of the biological name.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: NCERT states that the name of the author appears after the specific epithet, at the end of the name, in abbreviated form; Linn. indicates that Linnaeus first described the mango.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The number of characters shared by the members of a taxon increases as we move from species to kingdom. Reason (R): Higher categories include a larger number of organisms.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Shared characters decrease, not increase, as we go up the hierarchy, so A is false. Higher categories do include more organisms, so R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Families Felidae and Canidae are placed together in the order Carnivora. Reason (R): A family is a group of related genera.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Both statements are correct, but the definition of a family does not explain why two families are united into an order; the order is formed because the families share a few similar characters.

pyq.q: Distinguish between a taxon and a category with one example each.
pyq.answer: A category is a rank or level in the taxonomic hierarchy (species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom). A taxon is the actual group of organisms placed at that rank. For example, class is a category while Mammalia is a taxon at the level of class; genus is a category while Panthera is a taxon at the level of genus. (1 mark for the distinction, 1 mark for examples.)

pyq.q: Expand ICBN and ICZN. What is the purpose of these codes?
pyq.answer: ICBN: International Code for Botanical Nomenclature, which governs the naming of plants. ICZN: International Code of Zoological Nomenclature, which governs the naming of animals. Purpose: to provide agreed rules so that every organism receives a single scientific name that is accepted all over the world, ensuring that each organism has only one name and that no other organism has the same name.

pyq.q: How does systematics differ from taxonomy?
pyq.answer: Taxonomy deals with the characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature of organisms. Systematics includes all of these and, in addition, takes into account the evolutionary relationships between organisms. The word systematics comes from the Latin systema, meaning a systematic arrangement of organisms; Linnaeus used Systema Naturae as the title of his publication.

pyq.q: Write the scientific names of wheat and housefly, and name the family of each.
pyq.answer: Wheat: Triticum aestivum, family Poaceae. Housefly: Musca domestica, family Muscidae. (Underline the two words of each name separately; genus with a capital letter, specific epithet in small letters.)

pyq.q: Name the genus and family to which lion, tiger and cat belong. In which order are they placed?
pyq.answer: Lion (Panthera leo) and tiger (Panthera tigris) belong to the genus Panthera; the cat belongs to the genus Felis. All three are in the family Felidae, which is placed with the family Canidae (dogs) in the order Carnivora.

pyq.q: State the rules of binomial nomenclature with a suitable example.
pyq.answer:
Binomial nomenclature, given by Carolus Linnaeus, gives each organism a two-word name. The rules are:

  1. Biological names are generally in Latin and written in italics; they are Latinised or derived from Latin irrespective of their origin.
  2. The first word represents the genus and the second component denotes the specific epithet.
  3. Both words, when handwritten, are separately underlined, or printed in italics, to indicate their Latin origin.
  4. The first word denoting the genus starts with a capital letter while the specific epithet starts with a small letter.
  5. The name of the author appears after the specific epithet, at the end of the biological name, in abbreviated form.

Example: Mangifera indica Linn., the mango. Mangifera is the genus, indica the specific epithet, and Linn. shows that Linnaeus first described the species.

pyq.q: Why are living organisms classified, and why do the systems of classification keep changing?
pyq.answer:
Organisms are classified because their number (1.7 to 1.8 million known species) and diversity are so large that they cannot be studied individually. Grouping them into categories on the basis of shared characters makes their study convenient, lets the characters of a group be understood from a few members, allows identification and naming, and reveals relationships and evolutionary affinities between groups.

The systems keep changing because classification depends on the characters chosen. Early systems used a few external, easily observed characters. As information on internal structure, cell structure, development, biochemistry, genetics and evolutionary relationships accumulated, and as new organisms were discovered, the criteria were revised and the systems changed accordingly. Classification is therefore dynamic and improves with knowledge.

pyq.q: Write the taxonomic hierarchy of man from species to kingdom, naming each category and its taxon.
pyq.answer:
Species: Homo sapiens (specific epithet sapiens)
Genus: Homo
Family: Hominidae
Order: Primata
Class: Mammalia
Phylum: Chordata
Kingdom: Animalia
As we go from species to kingdom the number of common characters decreases and the number of organisms included increases.

pyq.q: Explain the terms species, genus and family, giving one plant and one animal example for each.
pyq.answer:
Species: a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities, distinguishable from closely related species by distinct morphological differences; the lowest category. Plant: Mangifera indica; animal: Panthera leo.

Genus: a group of related species with more characters in common than with species of other genera; an aggregate of closely related species. Plant: Solanum (potato and brinjal); animal: Panthera (lion, tiger, leopard).

Family: a group of related genera with fewer similarities than a genus, based in plants on both vegetative and reproductive features. Plant: Solanaceae (Solanum, Petunia, Datura); animal: Felidae (Panthera and Felis).

pyq.q: Explain what is meant by identification, nomenclature and classification. In what order are they carried out?
pyq.answer: Identification is determining the correct name and position of an organism by comparing its characters with those of already known organisms; it establishes which organism we are dealing with. Nomenclature is giving the organism a standardised scientific name, under ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals, so that it has one name recognised everywhere. Classification is grouping organisms into convenient categories (taxa) on the basis of easily observable shared characters and arranging the categories in a hierarchy. The order is identification first, then nomenclature, then classification, because an organism cannot be named until it is correctly identified and described, and it can be placed in the hierarchy only after it has been named and its characters are known. All three are processes basic to taxonomy.

pyq.q: Illustrate the taxonomic hierarchy with suitable examples of a plant and an animal. What happens to the number of shared characters and the number of organisms as we go up the hierarchy?
pyq.answer:
The taxonomic hierarchy is the arrangement of taxonomic categories in ascending order: species → genus → family → order → class → phylum (division in plants) → kingdom. Each category is a rank, and the group placed at each rank is a taxon.

Plant, mango: kingdom Plantae; division Angiospermae; class Dicotyledonae; order Sapindales; family Anacardiaceae; genus Mangifera; species indica. (Alternatively wheat: Plantae; Angiospermae; Monocotyledonae; Poales; Poaceae; Triticum; aestivum.)

Animal, man: kingdom Animalia; phylum Chordata; class Mammalia; order Primata; family Hominidae; genus Homo; species sapiens. (Alternatively housefly: Animalia; Arthropoda; Insecta; Diptera; Muscidae; Musca; domestica.)

As we go up from species to kingdom, the number of characters shared by the members of a taxon goes on decreasing, because each higher category unites more diverse groups on the basis of fewer common characters; at the same time the number of organisms included in the taxon increases, since a genus contains one or more species, a family several genera, and so on up to a kingdom that contains all the phyla. Consequently, the higher the category, the greater the difficulty of determining its relationship to other taxa at the same level, and classification becomes more complex.

pyq.q: What is nomenclature? Why is it necessary? Describe the system of binomial nomenclature with its rules and an example.
pyq.answer:
Nomenclature is the standardised naming of organisms so that a particular organism is known by the same name all over the world. It is necessary because local names differ from region to region and language to language; one organism may have many names and one name may refer to different organisms, which makes scientific communication impossible. Nomenclature is possible only after the organism has been correctly identified and described. Agreed rules for plants are given in the International Code for Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN) and for animals in the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN); these ensure that each organism has only one name and that no other organism has the same name.

Binomial nomenclature, given by Carolus Linnaeus, gives each organism a name with two components, the generic name and the specific epithet. Rules: (1) names are generally in Latin, written in italics, and are Latinised whatever their origin; (2) the first word is the genus and the second is the specific epithet; (3) both words are underlined separately when handwritten or printed in italics to show their Latin origin; (4) the genus begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter; (5) the author's abbreviated name is written after the specific epithet.

Example: Mangifera indica Linn. for the mango; Mangifera is the genus, indica the specific epithet, and Linn. indicates that Linnaeus first described the species. Other examples: Homo sapiens, Panthera leo, Solanum tuberosum.

pyq.q: Describe the seven taxonomic categories in ascending order with one example of each, using the genus Panthera and its related taxa wherever possible.
pyq.answer:
Species: a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities, the lowest category. Panthera leo (lion), Panthera tigris (tiger), Panthera pardus (leopard) are three species.

Genus: a group of related species with more characters in common than with species of other genera. Lion, tiger and leopard form the genus Panthera, which differs from the genus Felis (cats).

Family: a group of related genera with fewer similarities than a genus. Panthera and Felis are placed in the family Felidae; dogs, with some similarities and some differences, are placed in a separate family, Canidae.

Order: an assemblage of families showing a few similar characters. Felidae and Canidae are included in the order Carnivora.

Class: a group of related orders. Order Carnivora (tiger, cat, dog) and order Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) are placed in the class Mammalia, which has other orders as well.

Phylum: a group of related classes. Mammals, along with fishes, amphibians, reptiles and birds, are placed in the phylum Chordata on the basis of a notochord and a dorsal hollow neural system. In plants the equivalent category is division.

Kingdom: the highest category. All animal phyla are placed in the kingdom Animalia (plants in Plantae). Going up this sequence the shared characters decrease and the number of organisms increases.

pyq.q:
Read the table and answer the questions. The taxonomic categories of four organisms are: Man: Homo sapiens, Homo, Hominidae, Primata, Mammalia, Chordata, Animalia. Housefly: Musca domestica, Musca, Muscidae, Diptera, Insecta, Arthropoda, Animalia. Mango: Mangifera indica, Mangifera, Anacardiaceae, Sapindales, Dicotyledonae, Angiospermae, Plantae. Wheat: Triticum aestivum, Triticum, Poaceae, Poales, Monocotyledonae, Angiospermae, Plantae.
(i) Name the category to which Diptera and Sapindales belong.
(ii) Which two organisms share the largest number of categories, and which categories do they share?
(iii) Angiospermae is placed in which category, and what is this category called in animals?
(iv) Identify the specific epithet in the name of the housefly and state how the name should be written by hand.
pyq.answer:
(i) Diptera and Sapindales are both orders (Diptera of the housefly, Sapindales of the mango).

(ii) Mango and wheat share the most: both are in the division Angiospermae and the kingdom Plantae. Man and housefly share only the kingdom Animalia.

(iii) Angiospermae is a division, the category used for plants; in animals the equivalent category is the phylum.

(iv) In Musca domestica the specific epithet is domestica. By hand, the two words are underlined separately, Musca with a capital M and domestica beginning with a small letter.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Lion (Panthera leo), leopard (Panthera pardus) and tiger (Panthera tigris) share many features and are placed in one genus. The domestic cat belongs to a different genus, Felis. Both genera are placed in the family Felidae, which along with the family Canidae (dogs) forms the order Carnivora. Carnivora and Primata are two of the orders of the class Mammalia.
(i) Define a genus and state why the cat is not included in Panthera.
(ii) Name the category represented by Felidae and the plant family that NCERT uses as its parallel example.
(iii) Which of the taxa named in the passage contains the most organisms and which the fewest?
(iv) Name three animals that NCERT places in the order Primata.
pyq.answer:
(i) A genus is a group of related species that have more characters in common than they share with species of other genera. The cat differs from lion, tiger and leopard in enough characters that it is placed in a separate genus, Felis, though it shares the family characters with them.

(ii) Felidae is a family, a group of related genera. NCERT's plant example is the family Solanaceae, containing the genera Solanum, Petunia and Datura.

(iii) The class Mammalia contains the most organisms, since it includes Carnivora, Primata and other orders; a single species such as Panthera leo contains the fewest.

(iv) Monkey, gorilla and gibbon.

practice_mcq.q: Binomial nomenclature was given by
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT credits the two-word naming system to Carolus Linnaeus, who also used the title Systema Naturae.

practice_mcq.q: In Mangifera indica, the word indica is the
practice_mcq.explanation: The first word is the genus and the second is the specific epithet.

practice_mcq.q: When handwritten, the scientific name Homo sapiens should be
practice_mcq.explanation: Both words are separately underlined when handwritten, or printed in italics, to indicate their Latin origin.

practice_mcq.q: The lowest category of the taxonomic hierarchy is
practice_mcq.explanation: Species is at the lowest end of the hierarchy and is the basic unit of classification.

practice_mcq.q: The number of species known and described on earth is about
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT gives the range as 1.7 to 1.8 million known and described species, with many still undescribed.

practice_mcq.q: The order Polymoniales includes the families
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT places Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae in Polymoniales mainly on the basis of floral characters.

practice_mcq.q: The housefly belongs to the order
practice_mcq.explanation: Musca domestica: family Muscidae, order Diptera, class Insecta, phylum Arthropoda.

practice_mcq.q: Wheat belongs to the family
practice_mcq.explanation: Triticum aestivum is in the family Poaceae, order Poales, class Monocotyledonae.

practice_mcq.q: Mango is placed in the class
practice_mcq.explanation: Mango is a dicot: class Dicotyledonae, division Angiospermae; Sapindales is its order.

practice_mcq.q: The word systematics is derived from the Latin word
practice_mcq.explanation: Systema means a systematic arrangement of organisms; Linnaeus used Systema Naturae as the title of his publication.

practice_mcq.q: Fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are placed in the phylum Chordata on the basis of
options: presence of a notochord and a dorsal hollow neural system
presence of hair and mammary glands
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT names the notochord and the dorsal hollow neural system as the common features of Chordata.

practice_mcq.q: As we move up the taxonomic hierarchy, the number of organisms in a taxon
practice_mcq.explanation: A genus includes its species, a family its genera and so on, so higher taxa contain more organisms while sharing fewer characters.

practice_mcq.q: Monkey, gorilla and gibbon are placed by NCERT in the order
practice_mcq.explanation: The order Primata, comprising monkey, gorilla and gibbon, is placed in the class Mammalia along with the order Carnivora.

practice_mcq.q: The family to which human beings belong is
practice_mcq.explanation: Man: Homo sapiens, genus Homo, family Hominidae, order Primata.

practice_mcq.q: In Mangifera indica Linn., the word Linn. indicates that
options: the plant is native to Linnaeus's country
the name was rejected by Linnaeus
the plant belongs to the family Linnaceae
practice_mcq.explanation: The author's abbreviated name after the specific epithet shows who first described the species.

practice_mcq.q: The rules for naming animals are laid down by
practice_mcq.explanation: ICZN is the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature; ICBN is the botanical code.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a category and not a taxon?
practice_mcq.explanation: Family is a rank in the hierarchy; Mammalia, Solanaceae and Panthera are actual groups of organisms, that is, taxa.

practice_mcq.q: The three pairs of jointed legs that characterise insects define a group at the level of
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT uses insects as the example of a class; the housefly is in class Insecta.

practice_mcq.q: Which pair of genera is placed in the same family?
practice_mcq.explanation: Solanum, Petunia and Datura are in the family Solanaceae; Panthera and Felis are in Felidae.

practice_mcq.q: Which statement about the taxonomic hierarchy is correct?
options: Genus is a group of related families
Order is a group of related classes
Class is a group of related orders
Phylum is a group of related kingdoms
practice_mcq.explanation: The correct sequence is species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom; class includes related orders such as Primata and Carnivora.

common_mistakes: Writing the specific epithet with a capital letter (Mangifera Indica) or underlining the whole name with one line. Each word is underlined separately, the genus capitalised and the epithet in small letters; examiners deduct for every wrongly written name in the paper, not just in this chapter.
Writing 'phylum Angiospermae' for a plant. The plant category is division; phylum is used only for animals. The equivalence is a standard 1-mark question.
Reversing the trend: saying common characters increase as we go from species to kingdom. They decrease; it is the number of organisms that increases.
Confusing taxon and category, or treating them as synonyms. Category is the rank (family); taxon is the group at that rank (Solanaceae).
Giving taxonomy and systematics the same definition. Systematics adds the study of evolutionary relationships; without that phrase the distinction earns nothing.

Mixing up the NCERT examples across levels: Felidae and Canidae are families (in order Carnivora), not genera; Panthera and Felis are genera (in family Felidae); Primata and Carnivora are orders (in class Mammalia).
Skipping identification when explaining the processes of taxonomy. Identification precedes nomenclature; a name cannot be assigned until the organism is correctly identified.
Mis-spelling or misplacing the Table 1.1 entries, especially writing Sapindales for wheat or Poales for mango, or forgetting that both are in division Angiospermae but in different classes.
strategy:
This is a short chapter and the marks come from precision, not volume, so prepare it in two evenings. On the first evening read the NCERT text once slowly and copy out, in your own hand, the four rules of binomial nomenclature with the Mangifera indica Linn. example, the definitions of the seven categories with NCERT's exact examples, and Table 1.1 in full. Write each scientific name with the two words underlined separately; the habit you form here is marked in every biology paper you sit for the next two years.

On the second evening work from memory. Reproduce Table 1.1 as four flow charts, then check against the book. Write the taxon–category distinction, the taxonomy–systematics distinction and the two trends of the hierarchy (characters decrease, organisms increase) as 2-mark answers. Answer all eleven NCERT exercise questions in writing; Q1, Q2, Q5, Q6, Q7, Q9 and Q11 are the ones that turn up in school papers almost unchanged. Then do the exemplar short-answer items on Brassica campestris Linn., taxon versus category, and brinjal versus potato.

For the paper: expect one MCQ or Assertion–Reason (1 mark), one definition-type question (2 marks) and possibly a 3-mark question on nomenclature rules or a hierarchy. If a 5-mark question comes, it is Exercise Q11 in some form; draw the two flow charts, add the arrow annotation for decreasing shared characters, and finish with the sentence that classification becomes more complex at higher categories. Do not spend more than the marks allow on this chapter; the time is better used on Chapters 2 to 4 of the same unit, which carry more marks.
revision_checklist: I can state the number of known and described species (1.7–1.8 million) and define biodiversity.
I can write the four rules of binomial nomenclature and the rule about the author's name, with Mangifera indica Linn. as the example.
I can expand ICBN and ICZN and state what the codes ensure.
I can distinguish identification, nomenclature and classification and give their order.
I can distinguish taxonomy from systematics and give the origin of the word systematics.
I can distinguish a taxon from a category with examples.
I can write the seven categories in ascending order and state that division replaces phylum in plants.
I can state both trends of the hierarchy: shared characters decrease, number of organisms increases, relationships get harder to determine.
I can define species, genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom with NCERT's examples (Panthera and Felis, Solanaceae, Polymoniales, Carnivora, Primata, Mammalia, Chordata).
I can reproduce Table 1.1 for man, housefly, mango and wheat from memory.
I can write the scientific names of man, mango, wheat, housefly, potato, brinjal, lion, tiger and leopard correctly by hand.
I know the suffixes -aceae (plant family), -ales (plant order) and -idae (animal family).
I can name the two features that define phylum Chordata and the feature NCERT uses for the class of insects.
I can answer why organisms are classified and why classification systems keep changing, in 3 marks each.
I can explain what makes potato and brinjal separate species within Solanum.
